# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
# Review: *Two Years On* (Varden 24-month follow-up and Halden subset)

This is a strong follow-up. It adds a stricter hours measure, registers the mediation test before the outcome data, reports a decline in the effect plainly, and treats the two-office meeting audit with the right caution. It also confirms that the four long-follow-up studies in the meta-analysis were all uncontrolled and measured scheduled hours. That was the gap behind the meta-analysis's "no decay" claim.

The table arithmetic checks out:

| Check | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Per hour, timesheets | 0.966 / 0.88 | +9.8% ✓ |
| Per hour, logs | 0.966 / 0.89 | +8.5% ✓ |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 | 100% ✓ |
| Halden 11, hours | 34.9 / 40.3 | −13.4% ✓ |
| Halden 11, per hour | 96.8 / 86.6 | +11.8% ✓ |

The biggest problem is that the two hours measures don't fit together given what log-in time is said to measure. That matters for both the "unrecorded work" conclusion and the mediation result.

## 1. Log hours, timesheet hours and meeting time don't reconcile

The paper says system logs record "time staff are working on cases." If so, logs exclude meetings, but timesheets include them. A rough reconciliation, relative to control:

- **Timesheet hours** fell 12% of about 37.9, roughly **4.5 hours per week**.
- **Meeting time** fell by about **3.3 hours** relative to control (treated 7.4 → 3.9; control 7.2 → 7.0).
- **Case-working time** should then have fallen by only about 4.5 − 3.3 ≈ **1.2 hours**, around **4%** of a base of roughly 30.5 hours.

Logs instead show **−11%**. Either log-in time includes meetings and other non-case time, or something else was cut heavily, or the measures are being compared on different bases. This matters in two ways:

- **The "unrecorded work" conclusion.** Comparing a log fall of 11% with a timesheet fall of 12% only tests for unclaimed hours if the two measures cover the same activities. If they don't, the comparison says little about whether timesheets understate work.
- **What the mediation result means.** If meetings are inside the hours denominator, cutting them raises output per hour almost by definition: non-productive hours are removed while case work continues. That is still a real and useful finding, but it is closer to accounting than to a behavioural mechanism. If meetings are outside the denominator, the mechanism must be something else, such as less fragmented time. The paper should say which applies.

Two related questions:

- **Is there a baseline for the log measure?** The table shows "—" for logs at nine months, and the paper says the measure was "added." A difference-in-differences needs pre-period log data. System logs are probably stored historically, but the paper should confirm the −11% uses a true baseline.
- **Where did the baseline meeting figures come from?** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six. Baseline values of 7.4 and 7.2 now appear. If they were extracted from calendars afterwards, say so.

## 2. The mediation test confirms the hypothesis less independently than presented

Registering the test before the 24-month outcomes is a real improvement. But "survives a registered test" claims more than the design supports:

- **It is not a test on new data.** The hypothesis came from the same seven treated offices, and the 24-month analysis covers the months that produced the original r = 0.71. A pre-specified model guards against choosing the analysis to fit the result. It doesn't give an out-of-sample replication.
- **Effectively there are 7 treated offices, not hundreds of office-months.** Office-months within an office are not independent. A CI of 28–66% looks narrow for 14 clusters. The paper should state how the interval was computed, for example a bootstrap that resamples whole offices.
- **The shares may overlap.** Meetings and fatigue could be linked: fewer meetings might reduce fatigue. Shares that add exactly to 100% suggest any overlap was assigned somehow. The paper should say how.
- **The confounding assumption is a serious limitation.** The limitations section notes mediation assumes no unmeasured confounding, but this assumption carries the whole 47% figure. The most plausible confounder, managers who were more committed to the change both cutting meetings and pushing output, would inflate the meetings share. That point belongs with the result, not only in the limitations.

A fairer summary would be something like: "a pre-registered analysis on the original offices supports the meetings pathway; independent replication is still needed."

## 3. The Summary combines two changes in the decline estimate

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data." The 12.5% was measured with timesheets and the 8.5% with logs, so the drop mixes real decline with the switch of hours measure.

- The like-for-like decline is **12.5% → 9.8%**, about a fifth.
- 12.5% → 8.5% is about a third.
- Section 5 says "about a quarter," which matches neither.

Report the timesheet-to-timesheet comparison as the decline. The log figure can be the stricter 24-month level.

Two time points also can't show the trajectory. Monthly output exists, so a month-by-month plot would show whether the gain levelled off or is still falling. That is the real question about how long the effect lasts.

## 4. Cost is still missing for case-processing

The counter arm was ended on cost and service grounds, and the paper costs that decision (+9% per contact). Case-processing gets no equivalent. At 24 months, scheduled hours are down 20% but timesheet hours only about 12%. That implies around 3 hours of claimed overtime per person per week on top of unchanged salaries, while output per employee is 3.4% below control.

On the overtime assumptions I used for the nine-month report, cost per case is likely up by well over 10%. That is the number the county needs to decide whether to keep the arm. It should be reported, along with overtime rates and how much of the overtime was actually paid.

The +9% counter figure also needs its basis stated. Twelve percent more staff at full pay suggests about +12% cost per contact. The +9% is plausible if staff costs are only part of total cost per contact, but say so.

## 5. Halden subset: checks needed

- **The baseline hours figure.** The baseline of **40.3** for the 11 continuing organisations matches exactly the baseline the re-analysis reported for all **27** time-tracking organisations. The 11 are a subset of the 17 that had both records and time tracking, whose baseline was 40.4. Confirm the 11 are measured against their own baseline. Also confirm all 11 have time tracking, since only 17 of the 23 with records did.
- **When the reversions happened.** The original pilot reported that 3 retail and hospitality organisations reverted at the end of the pilot. Are the hospitality group and the retail chain here the same organisations, or did they revert later? The answer changes what "reverted by 24 months" means.
- **"All with client-facing or coverage obligations"** stretches the categories. A marketing agency citing client deadlines is not coverage-bound in the sense used throughout this literature, and the meta-analysis coding would class it as discretionary. As written, the Summary makes the reversion pattern look cleaner than it is. One of three reverters was in discretionary work.
- **Who replied.** Only 14 of 23 replied. Organisations doing well are more likely to supply data, and that is a third filter on top of the "survivors twice over" the paper already notes. The upper-bound framing is correct and should name this filter as well.

## 6. Smaller points

- **The meeting audit comparison:** comparing the two auditing control offices with their own previous six months doesn't account for seasonality or general trends. Comparing them with the other five control offices over the same months would be easy and much more informative.
- **Registration timing:** the nine-month report said the confirmatory test was already registered. This report says the protocol was filed at month 11. The dates are probably compatible, but stating both would avoid confusion.
- **Disclosure:** R. Okafor is a lead author of the Halden pilot whose claims this report partly revisits. That is fine, and it was probably necessary for data access, but a short competing-interests statement would help.
- **Section 5's response to the re-analysis and the meta-analysis** is fair and well judged. It credits the re-analysis's measurement points while rejecting its overreach, which is the right tone for a debate that has had overclaims on both sides.

## Where the five documents now leave the question

- **Discretionary work:** the best estimate of the per-hour gain is about **8–10% at two years**, down from about 12% at nine months on comparable measures. It rests mainly on a single controlled trial, which includes Varden's 7-versus-7 case-processing comparison. The 11 continuing Halden organisations (about 12%) set an upper bound.
- **Output per employee in discretionary work** is slightly below control, about −3%, with a CI that includes zero. **Cost per unit of output is unreported and probably higher.**
- **Coverage-bound work:** the result is clearly negative. One randomised arm was ended because of waiting times, and the costed fix is substantial.
- **Mechanism:** cutting meetings is the leading candidate, but how much it explains depends on the hours-measure question in section 1. It also needs testing in a design that reorganises work *without* cutting hours. The control-office audit hints that this could capture some of the gain.

I can draft a referee report on this follow-up, or turn the five-document synthesis into a briefing note.
